breakfast.name: Cafe Touba (Sacred Spiced Coffee)
ingredients: Coffee (Robusta beans -- roasted with Guinea pepper and djar)
Djar (cloves of the African pepper variety)
instructions: Cafe Touba is the sacred coffee of Senegal -- named after the holy city of Touba
Touba is the spiritual capital of the Mouride Brotherhood (Mouridism)
The Mouride Brotherhood: the most powerful Sufi order in West Africa
Founded by Sheikh Ahmadou Bamba in the late 19th century
Cafe Touba is not just coffee -- it is a spiritual and cultural statement
The Guinea pepper (selim) gives a smoky, peppery, resinous flavor unlike any other coffee
The djar (cloves-variant): another layer of spice complexity
Filtered through a cloth filter -- similar to West African tea-making technique
Drunk hot and sweet throughout the day -- not just at breakfast
Cafe Touba vendors are found at every Dakar street corner
The street vendor with the large thermos and small glasses: the Dakar morning
breakfast.description: The sacred coffee of Senegal -- Robusta beans roasted with Guinea pepper (selim, a smoky-resinous West African pepper) and djar, brewed and filtered through cloth. Named after Touba, the holy city of the Mouride Brotherhood (the most powerful Sufi order in West Africa). More than coffee: a spiritual and cultural statement. Street vendors with large thermoses define the Dakar morning.

breakfast.name: Thiakry (Millet Couscous Dessert-Breakfast)
ingredients: Sour cream or yoghurt (lait caille -- curdled milk)
instructions: Thiakry is the Senegalese sweet millet couscous -- served as breakfast or dessert
Millet: the grain of West Africa -- the pre-colonial grain before rice arrived
Thiakry uses steamed millet couscous (not wheat couscous -- entirely different texture)
The millet is steamed until light and fluffy
Mixed with lait caille (Senegalese curdled milk) -- slightly sour, creamy
Sweetened with sugar, perfumed with vanilla, spiced with nutmeg and cinnamon
Thiakry is one of the most beloved Senegalese sweet preparations
The combination of grain + sour dairy is the Sahelian food tradition
Also made with bissap (hibiscus) for a purple version -- festive
Served at celebrations, Tabaski (Eid al-Adha), and everyday breakfasts
breakfast.description: Senegalese sweet millet breakfast -- steamed millet couscous (thiakry, not wheat) mixed with lait caille (curdled milk, slightly sour), sweetened with sugar, vanilla, and spiced with nutmeg. Millet is the pre-colonial West African grain; this dish represents the Sahelian food tradition of grain + sour dairy. Served at Tabaski celebrations and everyday breakfasts.

breakfast.name: Lakh (Millet Porridge with Baobab)
ingredients: Baobab fruit powder (bouye -- the tangy white powder)
Milk or lait caille (optional -- to mix in)
instructions: Lakh is the Senegalese millet porridge -- a fundamental West African breakfast
Millet: the grain of the Sahel -- drought-resistant, ancient, nutritious
The porridge is made from millet flour cooked in water with constant stirring
Baobab fruit powder (bouye) is stirred in after cooking
Baobab: the tree of life across the Sahel -- the fruit has 6x the vitamin C of oranges
The bouye powder: white, tart, creamy-textured -- it changes the porridge completely
The combination of millet + baobab is ancient Sahelian food
Sweetened with sugar -- the sweetness balances the tartness of the baobab
Lait caille (curdled milk) can be stirred in -- the dairy-grain-baobab combination
Lakh is sold by women vendors at Dakar bus stops in the morning
breakfast.description: Senegalese millet porridge with baobab -- millet flour cooked in water, stirred with baobab fruit powder (bouye: tangy white powder, 6x the vitamin C of oranges), sweetened with sugar, enriched with curdled milk. The millet + baobab combination is ancient Sahelian food. Sold by women vendors at Dakar bus stops in the morning.

breakfast.name: French Bread and Butter (Colonial Legacy)
ingredients: French baguette (baguette -- fresh from Senegalese bakeries)
instructions: Senegal was a French colony for over a century -- 1677 to 1960
The French baguette is now a Senegalese daily necessity
Senegal produces some of the best baguettes in West Africa
The baguette in Dakar: fresh, crusty, available at every Dakar neighborhood bakery
Eaten with butter and Nescafe: the urban Senegalese breakfast
The colonial food legacy: adopted and adapted into Senegalese culture
Senegalese bakeries: often run by families since independence, maintaining quality
The baguette + cafe Touba combination: the hybrid Senegalese breakfast
French bread culture has deeply rooted in Senegal -- bought fresh daily like in Paris
breakfast.description: Colonial legacy in the Senegalese morning -- the French baguette, now a daily necessity, with butter and Nescafe. Senegal was a French colony from 1677 to 1960; the baguette stayed. Senegalese bakeries produce some of the best baguettes in West Africa, fresh daily like in Paris. The baguette + cafe Touba is the hybrid Senegalese urban breakfast.

lunch.name: Thieboudienne (Jollof Rice with Fish)
ingredients: Whole fish (thiof/grouper is the most prized) or fish pieces
Broken rice (toasted -- the Senegalese rice method)
instructions: Thieboudienne is the Senegalese national dish -- jollof rice with fish
The name: thieb = rice (in Wolof), dienne = fish
Thieboudienne is the origin of jollof rice -- before it spread across West Africa
The UNESCO recognition: Thieboudienne was awarded UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage status in 2021
Yeet: the dried fermented giant West African snail -- the essential umami ingredient
Neterou (dawadawa/locust beans): another fermented ingredient adding deep umami
The technique: fish is stuffed with a paste of parsley, scotch bonnet, garlic, and yeet
The stuffed fish is fried, then simmered in tomato-based broth
The broken rice is toasted in the same pan before adding the broth
A gentle layer of rice sticks to the bottom -- the xoon, the prized scorched rice
The xoon (crispy bottom rice): fought over at the table -- the Senegalese socarrat
Served on a communal platter -- everyone eats from the same large bowl
lunch.description: Senegalese national dish and UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage -- the origin of jollof rice. Whole fish (thiof/grouper) stuffed with a paste of parsley, scotch bonnet, garlic, and yeet (fermented mollusc, the umami), fried then simmered in tomato broth; broken rice toasted and cooked in the broth until the xoon (crispy bottom layer) forms. Served communally. The ancestor of West African jollof rice.

lunch.name: Mafe (Peanut Stew)
ingredients: Peanut butter (natural -- the base of the stew)
instructions: Mafe is the Senegalese peanut stew -- one of West Africa most beloved dishes
Peanut: the groundnut was brought to West Africa by Portuguese traders (via South America)
Now peanuts are as deeply West African as millet -- they are the cooking fat and protein
Mafe: peanut stew exists across West Africa under different names (groundnut soup)
The Senegalese mafe is typically with beef or lamb
The base: onion and tomato fried in palm oil
The peanut butter dissolved into the broth -- it thickens and enriches
The vegetables cooked until soft in the peanut broth
The flavor: rich, slightly sweet, slightly smoky from the palm oil
Served over white rice
Mafe is the second most important Senegalese dish after thieboudienne
lunch.description: Senegalese peanut stew -- beef or lamb simmered in a broth of peanut butter, tomato, and palm oil until the stew is rich, thick, and slightly sweet, with sweet potato, eggplant, and cabbage. Peanuts arrived via Portuguese traders from South America; now they are as deeply West African as millet. Mafe is the second Senegalese national dish after thieboudienne. Served over rice.

lunch.name: Yassa Poulet (Lemon Chicken)
ingredients: Onions (many -- the dish is mostly onion)
instructions: Yassa is the Casamance (southern Senegal) dish -- lemon and onion marinated chicken
Casamance: the southern region of Senegal, separated from the north by The Gambia
The lemon + onion marinade is the definition of yassa -- it is the dish
Marinate overnight: the chicken absorbs the lemon and onion flavors deeply
The caramelized onions: after marinating, the onions are slow-cooked until golden-soft
The chicken is first grilled (or pan-fried) until golden -- then added back to the onions
The marinade liquid is added back -- it reduces to a sauce
The mustard adds complexity to the lemon sauce
The scotch bonnet is kept whole -- it adds heat without making everything blazing
Yassa can be made with fish (yassa poisson) or lamb -- chicken is the most common
lunch.description: Casamance (southern Senegal) lemon-onion chicken -- chicken marinated overnight in lemon juice, onion, garlic, and mustard, grilled until golden, simmered with caramelized onions until the reduced marinade becomes a tangy, slightly sweet sauce. The scotch bonnet kept whole for heat without fire. Served over white rice. Yassa poisson (fish version) is equally beloved.

lunch.name: Superkanja (Okra Leaf Stew)
instructions: Superkanja is the Senegalese sticky okra stew -- from the Casamance and Diola tradition
The okra leaves (not pods) are the vegetable -- they create the characteristic stickiness
The stickiness is intentional and prized -- the viscous texture is the dish
Palm oil is the fat -- it gives the dark color and earthy flavor
Yeet (dried fermented mollusc) and guedj (dried smoked fish): the umami base
These fermented ingredients are essential to Senegalese cooking -- they replace the salt function
The Diola people of Casamance: the ethnic group most associated with this dish
Superkanja is served over rice -- the sticky okra sauce clinging to the grains
lunch.description: Senegalese sticky okra stew -- okra leaves (not pods) cooked in palm oil with yeet (dried fermented mollusc) and guedj (dried smoked fish) until viscous and dark. The stickiness is intentional and prized. Diola people of Casamance are most associated with this dish. The fermented ingredients replace the salt function and build deep umami. Served over rice.

lunch.name: Domoda (Gambian-Senegalese Peanut Stew)
instructions: Domoda is the peanut stew shared by Senegal and The Gambia
The Gambia is a small country entirely surrounded by Senegal -- sharing the Wolof culture
Domoda and mafe are essentially the same dish under different names
The Gambian version (domoda) tends to be slightly thicker and richer
Peanuts (groundnuts) in West Africa: oil crop, protein, and cooking base
The sweet potato adds sweetness and body
Scotch bonnet: the West African chili -- sharper heat than habanero
Served over rice -- the universal West African grain pairing
The dish reflects the Senegambia food zone: shared ingredients, shared techniques
lunch.description: Gambian-Senegalese peanut stew -- chicken or beef, peanut butter, tomato, sweet potato, and scotch bonnet in a thick, rich stew served over rice. The Gambia is entirely surrounded by Senegal; domoda and mafe are essentially the same dish under different names, reflecting the shared Wolof culture of the Senegambia food zone.

dinner.name: Thiebou Yapp (Meat Rice)
instructions: Thiebou yapp is the meat version of thieboudienne -- same technique, different protein
Thieb = rice, yapp = meat (in Wolof)
The same broken-toasted rice technique as thieboudienne
The lamb or beef simmered in tomato broth with vegetables
The rice cooked in the broth -- absorbing the meat and tomato flavors
The xoon (crispy bottom rice) forms here too -- the prized layer
Served communally on a large platter
Thiebou yapp is made when fish is unavailable or for meat-preferring guests
During Eid al-Adha (Tabaski in Senegal): thiebou yapp with lamb is everywhere
dinner.description: Senegalese meat rice -- the lamb or beef version of thieboudienne using the same broken-rice-toasted technique: meat simmered in tomato broth with vegetables, broken rice toasted in the same pan and cooked in the broth, xoon (crispy bottom layer) formed at the end. Communal platter. The Tabaski (Eid al-Adha) dish when the sacrificed lamb becomes the protein.

dinner.name: Cebu Jen (Another Name for Thieboudienne)
ingredients: Same as thieboudienne -- fish, broken rice, vegetables, yeet, tomato
instructions: Cebu jen is the Jola/Diola name for thieboudienne -- the same dish
Different ethnic groups in Senegal have different names for the same dish
The Wolof call it thieboudienne; the Jola/Diola call it cebu jen
Jola: the ethnic group of Casamance (southern Senegal and The Gambia)
The Jola version sometimes has slight differences in spice or fish preparation
The dish itself: essentially the same rice-and-fish combination
The naming reflects the ethnic diversity of Senegal -- Wolof, Serer, Fula, Jola, Mandinka
Wolof is the lingua franca of Senegal -- but not everyone is Wolof
dinner.description: The Jola/Diola name for Senegal national fish rice dish -- same preparation as thieboudienne (fish, broken rice, vegetables, tomato, yeet) but named cebu jen in the Casamance tradition. Reflects Senegalese ethnic diversity: Wolof, Serer, Fula, Jola, and Mandinka all have their food traditions within Senegalese cuisine. Wolof is the lingua franca but not everyone is Wolof.

dinner.name: Soupe Kandja (Okra and Palm Nut Soup)
ingredients: Palm nut cream (extracted from palm nuts)
instructions: Soupe kandja is the Senegalese palm nut and okra soup
Palm nut cream: extracted from the boiled and pressed red palm nuts
Different from palm oil: the cream includes the flesh of the palm nut, not just the oil
The palm nut cream gives the soup a deep reddish-orange color and rich, fruity-earthy flavor
The okra: sliced pods that thicken the soup with their natural mucilage
The double thickening: palm nut cream + okra mucilage
Smoked fish or dried fermented mollusc (yeet) for the umami base
This soup is similar to the palm nut soups of Sierra Leone, Ghana, and Nigeria
Served over white rice or fufu
The soup represents the forest zone of coastal Senegal -- palm tree country
dinner.description: Senegalese palm nut and okra soup -- palm nut cream (richer than palm oil: includes palm flesh) combined with sliced okra pods for double thickening, smoked fish and yeet (fermented mollusc) for umami. Deep reddish-orange from the palm fruit. Connects Senegal to the palm nut soup tradition of coastal West Africa from Sierra Leone to Nigeria. Served over rice or fufu.

dinner.name: Pastels (Senegalese Fish Fritters)
ingredients: Fish filling: flaked fish, onion, parsley, scotch bonnet, Dijon mustard, noodles
Thin pastry wrappers (spring roll skin or pastry dough)
instructions: Pastels are the Senegalese street food -- fish-filled fried pastries
The Lebanese influence on Senegalese cuisine: Lebanese merchants settled in Senegal
Pastels are influenced by Lebanese sambousek but fully Senegalized
The filling: flaked fish mixed with onion, parsley, scotch bonnet, and mustard
Some versions include cooked vermicelli noodles in the filling
Wrapped in thin pastry and deep-fried until golden
Sold at every Dakar street corner -- the Senegalese street snack
Eaten with dibi (Senegalese mustard) or simply hot from the fryer
Pastels are the Senegalese empanada -- the international fried pastry tradition meeting West Africa
dinner.description: Senegalese street food -- flaked fish mixed with onion, parsley, scotch bonnet, and Dijon mustard (Lebanese influence on Senegalese cuisine), wrapped in thin pastry and deep-fried golden. Sold at every Dakar street corner. The Senegalese version of the Lebanese sambousek, fully adapted to West African flavors. The most common Dakar street snack.

dinner.name: Caldou (White Fish and Lime)
ingredients: White fish fillets (thiof or other firm white fish)
instructions: Caldou is the simplest Senegalese fish dish -- white fish in lime and onion broth
The pure simplicity is the point -- it shows the quality of the fish
Thiof (grouper or white grouper): the most prized Senegalese fish
The lime juice brightens the broth -- the acidity is the dominant flavor
The scotch bonnet kept whole -- it perfumes the broth without making it fiery
Palm oil gives the broth its golden color and earthy richness
Caldou is quick -- fish is delicate and requires no long cooking
Served with white rice -- the broth poured over
The dish represents the coastal Senegalese fishing tradition
dinner.description: Simple Senegalese coastal fish dish -- white fish (thiof/grouper) cooked quickly in a lime, onion, and palm oil broth with a whole scotch bonnet for perfume. The purity shows the fish quality. Served over white rice with the broth poured over. Represents the straightforward cooking of the Senegalese fishing villages.

snacks.name: Bissap (Hibiscus Juice)
instructions: Bissap is the Senegalese hibiscus drink -- the most important West African cold drink
Bissap is the Wolof name; it is also called zobo (Nigeria), sobolo (Ghana), wonjo (Gambia)
Dried Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers: deep red-purple, intensely tart
Boiled in water then sweetened generously with sugar
The color: deep ruby red -- beautiful and striking
The flavor: intensely tart and slightly floral -- like berry juice with complexity
Mint added to the cooled juice -- the freshness
Served cold: the hot Dakar afternoon requires cold bissap
Bissap with ginger: a popular variation -- ginger + hibiscus is the sharpest combination
Sold by women vendors on Dakar streets in large plastic bags
snacks.description: West African hibiscus drink -- dried Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers boiled in water, sweetened, cooled, and served cold with mint. Deep ruby red, intensely tart. The universal West African cold drink: bissap in Wolof, zobo in Nigeria, sobolo in Ghana, wonjo in The Gambia. Sold by women vendors in Dakar streets in plastic bags. Ginger + hibiscus is the sharpest variation.

snacks.name: Ngalakh (Baobab and Peanut Dessert)
ingredients: Baobab fruit powder (bouye -- the tart white powder)
instructions: Ngalakh is the Senegalese festive dessert -- served at Christian celebrations
Senegal: a predominantly Muslim country with a significant Christian minority
The Lebou and Serer Christians of Dakar and Cape Verde area celebrate Pentecost with ngalakh
The baobab powder (bouye) provides the signature tartness
The peanut butter provides richness and binding
Mixed with millet couscous -- the grain of Senegal
Sweetened and spiced with vanilla and nutmeg
The result: a thick, fragrant, sweet-tart paste
Ngalakh is exchanged between Muslim and Christian neighbors at the celebration
The food represents the Senegalese teranga (hospitality) across religious lines
snacks.description: Senegalese festive dessert for Christian celebrations -- baobab fruit powder (tart), peanut butter (rich), and millet couscous mixed into a thick, fragrant paste, sweetened with sugar and spiced with vanilla and nutmeg. Exchanged between Muslim and Christian neighbors at Pentecost, representing the Senegalese teranga (hospitality) across religious lines.

snacks.name: Accara (Black-Eyed Pea Fritters)
instructions: Accara are the Senegalese black-eyed pea fritters -- the West African akara
Known as akara in Nigeria and Brazil (brought by the Yoruba diaspora across the Atlantic)
In Senegal: accara, a slight variation but essentially the same dish
Black-eyed peas soaked overnight, skins rubbed off -- the white batter underneath
Ground to a smooth batter with onion and scotch bonnet
The batter should be light and airy -- whipped to incorporate air
Dropped into hot oil -- they puff and become crispy
The interior: soft and slightly beany, slightly onion-flavored
Sold at Dakar markets in the morning -- the women frying accara in enormous pots
The akara/accara crossed the Atlantic with enslaved West Africans to Brazil and Cuba
snacks.description: Senegalese black-eyed pea fritters -- soaked peas with skins removed, ground to a smooth batter with onion and scotch bonnet, dropped into hot oil until puffed and crispy. The interior stays soft and beany. This fritter crossed the Atlantic with enslaved West Africans: akara in Nigeria and Brazil, accara in Senegal. Morning market food; women fry them in enormous pots.

snacks.name: Dibi (Grilled Lamb)
ingredients: Mustard sauce (Senegalese mustard -- more mustardy than French Dijon)
instructions: Dibi is Senegalese grilled lamb -- the street barbecue tradition
Dibiteries: the Senegalese barbecue shops -- usually run by Fula (Fulani) men
The Fula are traditionally cattle and sheep herders -- they know their meat
The lamb is grilled over charcoal until well-done (the Senegalese preference)
Served wrapped in newspaper or on a simple plate
Raw sliced onion alongside: the refreshing contrast to the grilled lamb
The Senegalese mustard sauce: thicker and more pungent than Dijon
Dibi is a nighttime food -- dibiteries open in the evening
Late-night Dakar: dibi with bissap or beer
snacks.description: Senegalese grilled lamb street food -- lamb shoulder or ribs grilled over charcoal at dibiteries (barbecue shops run by Fula herders), served with raw sliced onion and thick Senegalese mustard sauce. The Fula are traditional livestock herders who know their meat. Late-night food: dibiteries open in the evening. Dibi wrapped in newspaper with mustard is Dakar nightlife.

desserts.name: Theere (Millet Couscous Pudding)
instructions: Theere is another version of the millet couscous dessert tradition
Senegal has multiple millet couscous desserts -- the grain and dairy combination is repeated
Theere is slightly coarser than thiakry -- the couscous is less fine
Served with lait caille: the cultured milk base
Sweetened to taste -- Senegalese desserts are quite sweet
The Sahelian food principle: grain + sour dairy = complete nutrition and pleasure
Served at communal events: naming ceremonies, weddings, funerals
desserts.description: Senegalese millet couscous pudding -- steamed coarse millet couscous served with lait caille (curdled milk) and sugar. The Sahelian food principle: grain + sour dairy = complete nutrition. Slightly coarser than thiakry. Served at naming ceremonies, weddings, and communal events.

desserts.name: Pain de Singe (Baobab Fruit Juice)
ingredients: Baobab fruit (the white powder inside the pod -- bouye)
instructions: Pain de singe means monkey bread -- the French name for the baobab fruit
The baobab fruit: a large, hard-shelled pod containing a dry white powder
The powder dissolves in water to create a tart, creamy, nutritious drink
The flavor: tartness of citrus + creaminess of dairy + slight earthiness
The baobab tree is sacred across the Sahel -- it lives for thousands of years
Some Senegalese baobab trees are estimated to be 1,000+ years old
The baobab is called the tree of life -- every part is used
The leaves: eaten as a vegetable in soups
The bark: used medicinally and to make rope
Pain de singe is the original Senegalese refreshment -- pre-colonial
desserts.description: The original Senegalese refreshment -- baobab fruit powder (bouye: the white, dry, tart powder inside the hard pod) dissolved in water with sugar. Tastes: citrus tartness + slight creaminess + earthiness. The baobab (called monkey bread, pain de singe in French) is sacred: some trees are 1,000+ years old. Every part used. Pre-colonial, pre-cane sugar: the ancient West African drink.

desserts.name: Thiakry bi Ditax (Millet with Ditax Fruit)
ingredients: Ditax fruit (African velvet tamarind -- small, brown, tart)
instructions: Ditax (African velvet tamarind, Dialium guineense) is the small brown tart fruit
The fruit: covered in a thin brown shell, the sweet-tart powder inside eaten directly
Mixed with millet couscous for a complex sweet-tart dessert
The combination: grain + fruit tartness + dairy + sugar
Ditax is a Senegalese childhood memory -- children eat them straight from the tree
The tartness of ditax is more complex than regular tamarind -- earthy and fruity
desserts.description: Senegalese millet couscous with African velvet tamarind -- steamed millet mixed with ditax (Dialium guineense, small brown pods with sweet-tart powder inside), lait caille, and sugar. Ditax is a Senegalese childhood memory: children eat them straight from the tree. The earthy-fruity tartness of ditax is more complex than regular tamarind.

drinks.name: Attaya (Senegalese Tea Ceremony)
ingredients: Chinese gunpowder green tea (the specific tea)
instructions: Attaya is the Senegalese tea ceremony -- brought from Morocco and adapted
The tea is made in three rounds (tours): first, second, and third
First round: strong, very bitter -- prepared in a small kettle over charcoal
Second round: slightly less strong, some sugar added
Third round: the sweetest, minted, almost like mint tea
The pouring ritual: the tea is poured from height into the glasses, creating froth
The froth is considered essential -- the pouring back-and-forth to create it
The three-round attaya takes 1-2 hours -- the social gathering IS the point
No one leaves before the third round -- this is the social contract of attaya
Chinese gunpowder green tea (not black, not mint tea) is the specific tea
Attaya represents the Senegalese teranga (hospitality) -- the slow, shared time
drinks.description: Senegalese three-round tea ceremony -- Chinese gunpowder green tea brewed and poured three times (first: strong and bitter; second: less strong; third: sweet and minty), each round poured from height into small glasses to create froth. The ceremony takes 1-2 hours; no one leaves before the third round. The social contract of attaya. Represents the Senegalese teranga (hospitality).

drinks.name: Ginger Juice (Gnamakoudji)
ingredients: Optional: hibiscus (bissap) to deepen the color
instructions: Ginger juice (gnamakoudji in Wolof/French hybrid) is the spicy-sweet cold drink
Fresh ginger grated or blended and steeped in water
The ginger intensity: Senegalese ginger juice is strong -- the heat rises in the throat
Sugar sweetens the sharpness
Lemon juice adds acidity -- brightening the ginger
Served cold over ice
Gnamakoudji is the Senegalese digestif -- taken after meals for the ginger heat
The ginger aids digestion in the hot climate -- the traditional reasoning
Also mixed with bissap (hibiscus) for a red-hot combination
drinks.description: Senegalese spicy ginger cold drink -- fresh ginger steeped in water, sweetened, finished with lemon juice, served ice cold. Senegalese ginger juice is strong: the heat rises in the throat. The traditional digestif in hot climate; also mixed with bissap (hibiscus) for a red-hot combination. The Senegalese version of the West African spiced cold drink tradition.

drinks.name: Bouye (Baobab Juice)
instructions: Bouye is the baobab fruit juice -- the same powder as pain de singe but as a cold drink
The Senegalese everyday cold drink alongside bissap
Dissolve the powder in water -- it creates a milky-white suspension
Sweetened with sugar
Served cold or over ice
The flavor: tart, creamy, slightly earthly -- cooling in the Dakar heat
Bouye has very high nutritional value: vitamin C, calcium, potassium
The baobab is being marketed internationally as a superfood
For Senegalese it has been the everyday drink for centuries -- no superfood marketing needed
drinks.description: Senegalese everyday baobab drink -- baobab fruit powder dissolved in cold water with sugar into a milky-white, tart-creamy suspension. High in vitamin C, calcium, and potassium. The baobab is being marketed internationally as a superfood; for Senegalese it has been the everyday cold drink for centuries. The ancient West African refreshment alongside bissap.
